patient.chief_complaint: Brief shaking at worksite, now confused and unresponsive 45 minutes later, coworker reports he fell and hit his head
patient.hpi: A 48-year-old Black male construction foreman was brought to the emergency department by EMS after a witnessed fall at a construction worksite. His coworkers reported he had a brief tonic-clonic seizure lasting about 90 seconds while walking, fell to the ground, and struck the right side of his head on concrete. He was wearing no helmet (office area of the site). After the seizure stopped, he did not regain normal consciousness. EMS found him confused, agitated, GCS 10, with a visible right temporal laceration and scalp hematoma. He arrived 35 minutes after the fall. He has no prior history of seizures. Coworkers report he was acting normally at work today. No alcohol or drug use at the worksite per coworkers. He has a history of HIV infection, diagnosed 4 years ago, on antiretroviral therapy. His most recent CD4 count was 382 cells/mm3 (6 weeks ago), and his viral load was undetectable (<20 copies/mL). He takes bictegravir/emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (Biktarvy) daily. He also takes atorvastatin for hyperlipidemia. He has no known history of CNS opportunistic infections. His wife reports he was entirely well this morning with no complaints. No prior head trauma. Social history: former moderate drinker (quit 1 year ago), non-smoker, no illicit drugs.

eeg.impression: ABNORMAL EEG. NCSE from left temporal-parietal region despite right-sided head impact. Left hemisphere NCSE may represent contrecoup injury or pre-existing focus. Urgent structural imaging required. Benzodiazepine and AED treatment indicated for NCSE. Clinical correlation recommended.

ct.impression: 1. Left temporal hemorrhagic contusion (contrecoup injury) — explains left NCSE on EEG. 2. CRITICAL INCIDENTAL FINDING: left basal ganglia ring-enhancing lesion 2.1 cm on contrast CT — in HIV patient must urgently differentiate toxoplasmosis vs primary CNS lymphoma vs abscess. This lesion may be the PRIMARY etiology of the first seizure that led to the fall. MRI brain with gadolinium required urgently.
recommended_actions: Urgent MRI brain with gadolinium for characterization of ring-enhancing lesion
Infectious disease consultation for HIV-related CNS lesion management
Neurosurgery consultation for hemorrhagic contusion monitoring and possible biopsy of ring-enhancing lesion

interactions.description: No significant pharmacokinetic interactions between bictegravir and levetiracetam — levetiracetam is not hepatically metabolized and does not induce CYP enzymes

interactions.description: Pyrimethamine inhibits folate metabolism — leucovorin supplementation mandatory to prevent megaloblastic anemia and thrombocytopenia
interactions.clinical_recommendation: Co-administer leucovorin 10-20 mg daily with pyrimethamine; monitor CBC weekly

interactions.description: Tenofovir alafenamide and pyrimethamine have minimal interaction at standard doses

output.summary: Levetiracetam is ideal AED for HIV patients on cART (minimal drug interactions). Pyrimethamine requires leucovorin supplementation. Biktarvy should be continued and optimized. Avoid enzyme-inducing AEDs (phenytoin, carbamazepine) in HIV patients on cART — CYP induction reduces ART levels.

output.impression: NCSE controlled with initial AED treatment. Residual left temporal epileptiform burden. Continue monitoring and AED therapy. Primary structural causes (toxoplasmosis + contrecoup contusion) are the epileptogenic drivers. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Management of toxoplasmic encephalitis in HIV-infected adults
results.key_finding: First-line: pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + leucovorin x6 weeks. For sulfonamide allergy: pyrimethamine + clindamycin 600 mg IV/PO q6h + leucovorin is alternative first-line regimen. Maintenance therapy after acute treatment required. Imaging response at 2 weeks confirms diagnosis; biopsy if no improvement. IRIS (immune reconstitution) is a risk with cART optimization.

output.summary: CNS toxoplasmosis in HIV: pyrimethamine + clindamycin + leucovorin (sulfonamide allergy alternative). 6-week acute treatment then maintenance. Levetiracetam preferred for seizure prophylaxis (no CYP interactions with cART). Avoid enzyme-inducing AEDs (phenytoin, carbamazepine) — reduce cART levels.

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: CNS toxoplasmosis reactivation presenting as new-onset focal seizure with NCSE and traumatic head injury from seizure-related fall in HIV patient

differential.key_features: Ring-enhancing lesion in HIV patient; however MRS shows lipid/lactate without elevated choline; Toxoplasma IgG positive and CSF PCR positive; EBV CSF negative — toxoplasmosis confirmed
DWI shows peripheral restriction not central (abscess = central restriction); Toxoplasma PCR positive; no fever; no source of bacteremia
No subdural on CT; contrecoup contusion explains left NCSE but ring-enhancing basal ganglia lesion is non-traumatic; toxoplasmosis is the primary pathology

critical_actions: CT head immediately to exclude epidural/subdural hematoma and identify ring-enhancing lesion
Levetiracetam for AED — do NOT use phenytoin or carbamazepine (CYP induction reduces cART levels)
Serum Toxoplasma IgG and CSF Toxoplasma PCR for diagnosis
Pyrimethamine + clindamycin + leucovorin (sulfonamide allergy — cannot use sulfadiazine)
Leucovorin mandatory with pyrimethamine — prevents megaloblastic anemia
Continue cART — do NOT stop antiretroviral therapy
contraindicated_actions: Phenytoin or carbamazepine for seizure prophylaxis in HIV patient on cART — CYP3A4 induction reduces bictegravir and other antiretroviral levels dramatically
Sulfadiazine — sulfonamide allergy; use clindamycin as alternative
Stopping cART — continuation essential for immune reconstitution and toxoplasmosis control
Delaying toxoplasmosis treatment to await biopsy — empiric treatment for 2 weeks is standard; biopsy only if no response
key_reasoning_points: New seizure in HIV patient = CNS structural lesion until proven otherwise — ring-enhancing lesion is toxoplasmosis at CD4 382
Enzyme-inducing AEDs (phenytoin, carbamazepine, valproate to a lesser extent) reduce antiretroviral levels — levetiracetam is the safe AED in HIV
Sulfonamide allergy precludes sulfadiazine — clindamycin is the established alternative for CNS toxoplasmosis
Leucovorin is mandatory with pyrimethamine to prevent bone marrow toxicity — not optional
The contrecoup contusion explains the left NCSE on EEG — the right-sided head impact caused left temporal cortical seizure focus, not the basal ganglia toxoplasmosis lesion directly
Ring-enhancing lesion identified incidentally — it likely caused the first seizure that led to the fall; this is the primary diagnosis

metadata.teaching_points: HIV + ring-enhancing lesion = toxoplasmosis workup; enzyme-inducing AEDs reduce cART; sulfonamide allergy alternative (clindamycin); leucovorin mandatory
metadata.pitfalls: Using phenytoin or carbamazepine in HIV patient; forgetting leucovorin; using sulfadiazine in sulfonamide allergy; attributing NCSE only to trauma without investigating ring-enhancing lesion
metadata.clinical_pearl: New seizure + ring-enhancing lesion + HIV + Toxoplasma IgG positive = treat empirically for 2 weeks. Use levetiracetam (no CYP). Avoid phenytoin/CBZ with cART. Sulfonamide allergy = pyrimethamine + clindamycin + leucovorin.
